questions.question_text: A particle is projected from the origin with speed $V$ at an angle $\alpha$ to the horizontal. After $2$ seconds its position vector is $14\underset{\sim}{i} + 6\underset{\sim}{j}$. Taking $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$, what is $V$, to $1$ decimal place?

options.why: Left the $-5t^{2}$ term out of the vertical equation, giving $V\sin\alpha = 3$ instead of $13$.
Treated the displacement components $14$ and $6$ as the velocity components, forgetting to divide by $t = 2$.
Added the two velocity components instead of using $\sqrt{(V\cos\alpha)^{2} + (V\sin\alpha)^{2}}$.

questions.question_text: A ball is projected from level ground at $60^{\circ}$ to the horizontal and lands $6$ seconds later. Taking $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$, what is its speed of projection, to $1$ decimal place?

options.why: Used $V\sin 60^{\circ} = gt$ with the full flight time, forgetting that the flight time is twice the time to the greatest height.
Used $\cos 60^{\circ}$ instead of $\sin 60^{\circ}$ for the vertical component.
Used $\cos 60^{\circ}$ for the vertical component and also forgot to halve the flight time.

questions.solution_text:
$y = -5t^{2} + Vt\sin 60^{\circ}$
The ball lands when $y = 0$ and $t = 6$.
$0 = -5(6)^{2} + 6V\sin 60^{\circ}$
$180 = 6V\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$
$V = \dfrac{60}{\sqrt{3}}$
$= 34.6\text{ m/s}$

questions.question_text: A ball is projected from level ground at $20\text{ m/s}$ and lands $30\text{ m}$ away. Taking $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$, what are the two possible angles of projection, to $1$ decimal place?

options.why: Stopped at the two values of $2\theta$ without halving them.
Halved the first solution but took the second as $180^{\circ} - 24.3^{\circ}$ instead of halving $131.4^{\circ}$.
Halved the two correct angles a second time.

questions.question_text: A ball is projected from level ground at $15\text{ m/s}$ and reaches a greatest height of $5\text{ m}$. Taking $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$, what is its angle of projection, to $1$ decimal place?

options.why: Used $H = \dfrac{V^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}{g}$, leaving the factor of $2$ out of the denominator.
Took the inverse sine of $\sin^{2}\theta = 0.4444$ without first taking the square root.
Left the factor of $2$ out of the denominator and also failed to take the square root.

questions.question_text: A particle is projected from the origin at $30\text{ m/s}$ at an angle $\theta$ and passes through the point $(45, 15)$. Taking $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$, what are the two possible values of $\theta$, to $1$ decimal place?

options.why: Used $\sec^{2}\theta = \tan^{2}\theta - 1$ instead of $1 + \tan^{2}\theta$.
Treated the roots of the quadratic as $\tan 2\theta$ and halved the resulting angles.
Took the second angle as the complement of the first; complementary angles give the same range, not the same point.

questions.solution_text:
1. **Write the horizontal and vertical equations of motion**
$x = 30t\cos\theta$, $y = -5t^{2} + 30t\sin\theta$
2. **Solve the horizontal equation for the time**
$45 = 30t\cos\theta$
$t = \dfrac{1.5}{\cos\theta}$
3. **Substitute the time into the vertical equation**
$15 = -5\left(\dfrac{1.5}{\cos\theta}\right)^{2} + 30\sin\theta\left(\dfrac{1.5}{\cos\theta}\right)$
$15 = -11.25\sec^{2}\theta + 45\tan\theta$
4. **Solve the resulting equation for the unknown**
$15 = -11.25\left(1 + \tan^{2}\theta\right) + 45\tan\theta$
$11.25\tan^{2}\theta - 45\tan\theta + 26.25 = 0$
$3\tan^{2}\theta - 12\tan\theta + 7 = 0$
$\tan\theta = \dfrac{12 \pm \sqrt{144 - 84}}{6}$
$= 0.7090\ldots$ or $3.2909\ldots$
$\theta = 35.3^{\circ}$ or $73.1^{\circ}$

questions.question_text: A ball is thrown from level ground at $30^{\circ}$ to the horizontal and just passes over a fence $3\text{ m}$ high standing $12\text{ m}$ away. Taking $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$, what is its speed of projection, to $1$ decimal place?

options.why: Wrote $\sin^{2}30^{\circ}$ in place of $\cos^{2}30^{\circ}$ when squaring $t = \dfrac{12}{V\cos 30^{\circ}}$.
Used $gt^{2}$ rather than $\frac{1}{2}gt^{2}$ in the vertical equation.
Used $gt^{2}$ instead of $\frac{1}{2}gt^{2}$ and also squared $\sin 30^{\circ}$ instead of $\cos 30^{\circ}$.

questions.solution_text:
1. **Write the horizontal and vertical equations of motion**
$x = Vt\cos 30^{\circ}$, $y = -5t^{2} + Vt\sin 30^{\circ}$
2. **Solve the horizontal equation for the time**
$12 = Vt\cos 30^{\circ}$
$t = \dfrac{12}{V\cos 30^{\circ}}$
3. **Substitute the time into the vertical equation**
$3 = -\dfrac{720}{V^{2}\cos^{2}30^{\circ}} + 12\tan 30^{\circ}$
$3 = -\dfrac{720}{0.75V^{2}} + 6.9282\ldots$
4. **Solve the resulting equation for the unknown**
$\dfrac{960}{V^{2}} = 3.9282\ldots$
$V^{2} = 244.3\ldots$
$V = 15.6\text{ m/s}$

questions.question_text: A stone is thrown from the top of a $30\text{ m}$ cliff at $45^{\circ}$ above the horizontal and hits the sea $4$ seconds later. Taking the launch point as the origin and $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$, what is its speed of projection, to $1$ decimal place?

options.why: Set $y = 0$ at landing, ignoring that the sea is $30\text{ m}$ below the launch point.
Set $y = +30$ instead of $y = -30$, adding the cliff height rather than subtracting it.
Left out $\sin 45^{\circ}$, using $V$ itself as the initial vertical velocity.

questions.question_text: A particle is projected from the origin with speed $V$ at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal, and the highest point of its path is $(24, 18)$. Taking $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$, what is $V$, to $1$ decimal place?

options.why: Took $\tan\theta = \dfrac{18}{24}$ from the coordinates of the point, which gives the direction of the displacement, not the direction of projection.
Used $\sqrt{24^{2} + 18^{2}}$, treating the length of the position vector as the speed.
Found only the vertical component $V\sin\theta = \sqrt{360}$ and ignored the horizontal component.

questions.solution_text:
At the greatest height $\dot{y} = 0$, so $t = \dfrac{V\sin\theta}{10}$.
$y = \dfrac{V^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}{20} = 18$
$V^{2}\sin^{2}\theta = 360$
$x = V\cos\theta \times \dfrac{V\sin\theta}{10} = 24$
$V^{2}\sin\theta\cos\theta = 240$
Dividing the first result by the second,
$\tan\theta = 1.5$
$\theta = 56.30^{\circ}\ldots$
$V^{2} = \dfrac{360}{\sin^{2}\theta}$
$= 520$
$V = 22.8\text{ m/s}$
